title: Exodos (lines 1233–1544)

teacherSummary.text: A second messenger reports offstage events at the palace. The blinded Oedipus enters and laments. He names Apollo as the cause and his own hand as the agent (lines 1343–1346; the blinding is self-harm reported offstage, taught as drama with context), and accepts the guilt as his alone to bear (lines 1418–1420). Creon arrives, does not mock him, and brings his daughters to him. Oedipus asks to be sent into exile and commends his daughters to Creon. The Chorus ends: count no one happy until his life is over.

segments.activity: Model the close reading of the anchor quotation using the written think-aloud below.
segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Not Ister nor all Phasis’ flood, I ween, / Could wash away the blood-stains from this house, / The ills it shrouds or soon will bring to light, / Ills wrought of malice, not unwittingly.” slowly and put it in my own words: The Second Messenger says that not even the great rivers Ister and Phasis could wash the blood from the royal house, and that new ills, done on purpose, are about to come to light. Next, craft. I notice the rivers are hyperbole, and the last line sets malice against unwittingly, chosen acts against the unknowing crimes of the past. The strongest word is “unwittingly”: the earlier crimes were done without knowledge; what follows is chosen. Then, effect. What does the contrast between malice and unwittingly add to the messenger's report? My answer: The contrast between malice and unwittingly prepares the report: the old crimes were done without knowledge, but the acts the messenger is about to describe were chosen, so the audience is warned before he speaks.

segments.script: Annotate the scene for characterization, theme (three marks with a margin note each), then write one claim-evidence-reasoning paragraph: what does this scene suggest about responsibility, mercy and the end? Then start your writing prompt at your assigned level (HS Sophomore: Analyze how Exodos (lines 1233–1544) develops the idea of responsibility, mercy and the end. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.) Exemplar: Oedipus takes responsibility while naming fate. Creon's restraint models mercy. The ending is grief with care, not despair. When the text says “Apollo, friend, Apollo, he it was / That brought these ills to pass; / But the right hand that dealt the blow / Was mine, none other” (Exodos (lines 1233–1544), Oedipus), it shows this directly. A second messenger reports offstage events at the palace. The blinded Oedipus enters and laments. He names Apollo as the cause and his own hand as the agent (lines 1343–1346; the blinding is self-harm reported offstage, taught as drama with context), and accepts the guilt as his alone to bear (lines 1418–1420). Creon arrives, does not mock him, and brings his daughters to him. Oedipus asks to be sent into exile and commends his daughters to Creon. The Chorus ends: count no one happy until his life is over.

framing.script: Teacher reads aloud before the reading. What happens: in this last part of the play a messenger reports that Queen Jocasta, having understood the truth, has taken her own life inside the palace. The method lines (1278–1281) are read as part of the text but are cited by line number only in our discussion and in every task. Oedipus then blinds himself, which is also reported, and the play shows us his grief. Context: in Greek tragedy such events happen offstage and are reported by a messenger. The play does not present Jocasta's death as noble or as a solution; it shows it as the ruin of a family. Self-harm is wrong, and it is never the answer to pain.
